rv.q: My only niggle was the needless air-battle footage projected at the end of each half. But Mark Thompson’s set is a comic-book delight, featuring a huge David Hockney-ish vista of the Sussex Downs. It perfectly distils the comic tone and is a rare blast of sunshine at the National.

It’s hilarious, if exhausting. Here, the verbal misplacings of Caroline Quentin’s Mrs Malaprop have a smutty edge. “Flatulence will get you everywhere,” is one of the milder examples, though she also mixes up “clematis” and “clitoris” and talks about “passing a significant millstone” on her birthday.

The National has a summer hit on its hands. I’d better add that I was one of the grumps who found Bean’s rewrite of Goldoni’s The Servant of Two Masters more than a little wearing. So it’s even more of a pleasure to report that this venture — anchored by Caroline Quentin as an adorable, potty-mouthed Mrs Malaprop — is a joyous romp.

Here, the pretensions that Bean and Chris target are a little different. Lydia Languish (Natalie Simpson) is an upper-class pilot whose role has filled her with a new egalitarian fervour: she experiments with treating her maid Lucy (Kerry Howard) like a human being and dreams of opening a lemon farm in Barnsley, to bring the refined joys of citr...

This nod to the role soldiers from the Commonwealth played in the war is one of the play’s strengths. Bean and Chris regularly use Lucy to undercut things (which Howard has great fun doing) and remind the audience of the characters’ relative privilege to one another and the differing stakes faced by characters from different backgrounds.

The result is a qualified triumph of an evening, one that pitches from the heights of comic delight – ‘‘What’s going to happen in England after we’ve won this war?’ ‘Bunting. Bunting everywhere’’ – to the lows of relentless and tiresome nudge-nudge-wink-wink.

What’s frustrating about the class stuff is how near the play comes to hitting the bullseye without ultimately displaying any real interest in doing so. Its simmering antiestablishmentarianism never builds: astringently funny lines are ultimately tossed away for yucks.
